analysis.one_liner: Restricts aggressive medical debt collection and forces hospitals to disclose their collection practices.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a Senate floor vote and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would limit how hospitals and their debt collectors go after patients for medical bills. Hospitals would have to wait 180 days after the first bill before taking harsh steps like garnishing wages, putting liens on homes, or suing. They would have to check whether a patient qualifies for charity care or public insurance first, cap interest on medical debt at 5% a year, and send patients itemized bills and payment receipts. Hospitals would also have to file public reports about which debt collectors they use and how many lawsuits, garnishments, and credit reports they pursue. Anyone hurt by violations could sue, and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau would have to report publicly on the medical debt industry.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients facing medical bills — especially uninsured and lower-income patients — gain a waiting period before harsh collection tactics, a check for charity care eligibility first, a low interest cap, itemized bills, and public data about which hospitals and collectors pursue lawsuits and garnishments.

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals and their debt collectors could not take 'extraordinary collection actions' — wage garnishment, bank account attachments, liens, lawsuits, or credit reporting — until 180 days after the first bill is sent [S3].

Hospitals could not start collections until they checked whether the patient qualifies for Medicaid, another public program, or the hospital's own charity care, and they would have to refer patients to that assistance [S3].
Interest on medical debt would be capped at 5% a year (or a lower federal judgment rate), and collections would be halted while a patient's insurance appeal is pending [S3].
Patients would receive an easy-to-understand itemized statement before collection starts and detailed payment receipts within 30 days of payment [S3].

Nonprofit hospitals could not collect more from uninsured patients than the amount 'generally billed' to insured patients, extending an existing nonprofit-hospital rule to enforcement through the bill's penalties [S3].

Hospitals would file annual public reports naming their debt collectors, describing how they compensate them, and counting the garnishments, liens, lawsuits, and credit reports they pursue, with a zip-code breakdown of referred accounts; the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau would report publicly on the industry using this data [S3].
Patients who are treated in violation of the rules could recover actual damages plus up to $1,000 per violation, with attorney's fees available in successful cases [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals (including nonprofit and for-profit systems) and the medical debt collection industry would face tighter collection limits, lower interest, mandatory charity-care screening, and new public reporting on their collection practices.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves the underlying bills themselves untouched: it regulates collection timing, interest, and disclosure, but a patient can still owe the full charges, so it eases the collection process without reducing what hospitals charge in the first place [S2] [S3].
The 180-day waiting period applies only to 'extraordinary' collection actions; ordinary phone calls and collection letters could still begin sooner, so day-to-day collection pressure continues [S3].

Hospitals and provider groups would argue the compliance burden is real: building itemized-billing, eligibility-screening, and annual reporting systems costs money, and for smaller providers those costs could add to the prices patients are billed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the protections are real but partial: collections would slow down, interest would be capped, charity care would be screened before lawsuits, and collection practices would become public — yet the core problem of what hospitals charge is left alone, and routine collection contacts could still start immediately. The main costs fall on hospitals and collectors as compliance and enforcement burden. On balance the bill would shift leverage from collectors toward patients, though its remedies are modest relative to the scale of medical debt in the United States.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2020, read twice, and sent to the Senate Health Committee, which took no action before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Christopher Murphy introduced the bill in the Senate on September 24, 2020, with Sen. Van Hollen as its sole cosponsor [S1] [S3] [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced [S5].
No hearing, markup, or vote followed, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and medical debt collectors are better off: the bill never advanced, so no new limits were placed on garnishments, liens, lawsuits, or interest on medical debt.

for.name: Sen. Christopher Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it referred to the Senate Health Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee where the bill sat unactioned (chair: Sen. Lamar Alexander, R-TN)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 24, 2020 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan split never came into view; both supporters were Democrats and the bill died in a Republican-chaired committee without any recorded opposition.

industries.note: The bill's rules — a 180-day waiting period before garnishments, liens, and lawsuits, charity-care checks first, and public reporting on collectors and their recovery rates — directly curtail how debt collectors operate and profit. Their business depends on aggressive collection from patients.

Hospitals would face mandatory charity-care screening, itemized billing, an interest cap, and annual public reports on their collection tactics. They keep the ability to bill and collect, and the bill regulates only collection practices rather than charges, so their revenue model survives — but with new compliance costs and public exposure of their collection data.

industries.industry: Credit reporting bureaus and consumer reporting agencies
industries.note: Delayed and reduced reporting of medical debts to credit bureaus (a listed extraordinary collection action) plus CFPB reporting drawing on anonymized bureau data would trim the flow of medical debt information that feeds consumer credit files.
